nameStory: The genus name 'Corophium' comes from Greek words meaning 'sweep' or 'broom,' referring to how these tiny crustaceans use their feathery antennae to sweep food particles from the water. The species name 'volutator' means 'roller' in Latin, describing their characteristic way of curling up into a ball when disturbed.
description: The mudflat amphipod is a tiny shrimp-like crustacean that lives in coastal mudflats and salt marshes. These small creatures are typically only a few millimeters long and have a curved, comma-shaped body when viewed from the side. They're semi-transparent to pale brown in color and have long, feathery antennae that are longer than their bodies. Despite their small size, they can be incredibly abundant, sometimes numbering in the thousands per square foot of mudflat.

idTips.label: Body shape
idTips.description: Distinctive curved, comma-like profile when viewed from the side, with a humped back that gives it an almost question-mark appearance

idTips.label: Antennae
idTips.description: Two long, feathery antennae that extend well beyond the body length and feel delicate to the touch

idTips.label: Color
idTips.description: Semi-transparent to pale brown coloration that makes them blend into muddy sediments

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Tiny creatures, typically 3-8 millimeters long - about the size of a grain of rice

idTips.label: Movement
idTips.description: Curls into a tight ball when disturbed, then quickly uncurls and swims with jerky, darting motions

habitat: Found in soft, muddy sediments of salt marshes, tidal creeks, and protected mudflats along the New England coast. They prefer areas with fine, organic-rich mud that feels smooth and slightly squishy underfoot, typically in the mid to upper intertidal zone where the salinity is moderate.

seasonality.spring: Most active as water temperatures warm, making this the best time to spot them swimming in shallow tidal pools. Look for them in recently flooded mudflats during incoming tides.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when they're most abundant and easiest to find. Turn over small chunks of mud near the surface to reveal their U-shaped burrows and the amphipods themselves.
seasonality.fall: Still active but beginning to move deeper into sediments. Best found by gently disturbing the top layer of mud during low tide.
seasonality.winter: Much less active and harder to find as they burrow deeper into the mud to avoid freezing. Rarely seen at the surface during this season.

funFact: These tiny mud-dwellers are ecosystem engineers that can completely transform their environment - in high densities, their constant burrowing can turn solid mudflats into a honeycomb of tunnels, actually changing the physical structure of the shoreline and affecting water flow patterns.
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with other small amphipods or tiny shrimp, but the distinctive curved, comma-shaped body profile is unique. Remember: if it looks like a tiny translucent question mark that curls into a ball when poked, it's likely a mudflat amphipod.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'mudflat amphipods,' these creatures are actually more closely related to terrestrial pill bugs than to true shrimp. This species was originally native to European coasts but was accidentally introduced to New England waters, likely through ballast water from ships.
compareHints: As the only Corophium species commonly found in New England mudflats, it's most similar to other small tube-dwelling amphipods in the same family. However, mudflat amphipods are distinguished by their more pronounced curved body shape and their habit of building U-shaped burrows rather than straight tubes. Other amphipods in the area tend to be more laterally compressed and less curved in profile.
